strengths: The paper addresses a genuine and practically important problem: extracting training signal from expert human solutions on problems where RLVR yields zero advantage, a setting where standard SFT/rationalization baselines demonstrably fail (Figure 3, Figure 6).

The proposed method is well-motivated and decomposed cleanly: (1) in-distribution trace generation via a 'privileged student' with mixed policy rollouts (inspired by speculative decoding and DAgger-style interactive imitation), and (2) a contrastive objective that penalizes rationalization shortcuts via an automatically constructed negative reference. Each component is ablated (Figures 5, 7, Table 4), and the ablations support the design choices.

Evaluation is unusually thorough for this area: multiple model families (Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct, Qwen3-8B think, plus weaker models in Figure 16), multiple benchmarks including out-of-domain (GPQA-Diamond, Table 1), token-budget-constrained evaluation with budget forcing (Figure 4), temperature-controlled baselines, RLVR baselines (GRPO, NuRL, DeepScaleR), and a generalization-gap analysis (Figure 6) that directly supports the shortcut-learning hypothesis.

The paper is commendably transparent about limitations: post-hoc deduplication analysis for IMO-AnswerBench leakage (Figure 14), honest reporting that weaker models (Qwen3-4B, R1-Distill-7B) show mixed results, and the observation that mixed policy rollouts slightly underperform direct sampling for non-reasoning models.
Release of a new resource (el-proof, 669 expert-authored Olympiad proofs with permission) and substantial training-efficiency gains (0.1 vs 277.6 H100 hours/epoch) add practical value.
The test-time efficiency finding (2-4x fewer tokens at matched performance) is a useful and non-obvious benefit of aligning to expert solution structure.
weaknesses: Some methodological choices are ad-hoc and weakly justified: the negative reference is constructed via regular-expression extraction of numeric/symbolic waypoints, which is math-domain-specific; the mixed policy rollout truncation length of 256 tokens is selected 'qualitatively'; and tau=0.8 is calibrated on training-set performance rather than a validation set. The generality of these heuristics beyond competition math is unclear.

The contrastive objective has limited theoretical grounding. The authors note the negative KL term is theoretically unbounded and appeal to empirical stability (Appendix B.5); a more principled analysis or at least failure-mode characterization would strengthen the contribution.

Single-seed results with no error bars or statistical significance testing. Given benchmark sizes (60 problems for AIME 2024/2025, 198 for GPQA-Diamond), some reported gaps (e.g., the ~1% pass@128 difference between generation methods) may not be statistically meaningful.

Hyperparameter transfer is questionable: gamma=0.1 was tuned once on Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct with a pass@128 selection metric and reused for all models/settings, and the authors themselves speculate this hurt weaker models (Figure 16). This limits confidence in the method's plug-and-play applicability.

The headline 'first demonstration' claim is difficult to verify given rapidly moving concurrent work (e.g., Bread, self-distillation approaches cited in Related Works), and the positioning against concurrent hint-based RLVR methods could be sharper.

Reproducibility is partially undermined by placeholder fields in the paper ('Our code is available at', 'Our extracted training dataset is available at' are left blank), so reproducibility currently rests on appendix details alone.

The claim that improvements reflect 'learning expert insights' would be strengthened by qualitative analysis of what the trained model actually does differently (e.g., examples of avoided shortcuts on test problems), rather than relying solely on aggregate pass@k evidence and the train/test generalization gap.

strengths: The paper addresses a well-motivated and practically important problem: extracting training signal from high-cost expert solutions on problems where RLVR yields zero advantage (exploration bottleneck on hard problems).

The method is coherently designed: the two-stage decomposition (in-distribution expansion via privileged-student rollouts, then a contrastive objective to suppress rationalization shortcuts) directly targets the two identified failure modes (didactic shortcuts from experts, rationalization shortcuts introduced by the model itself), and Figure 1 provides a clear illustrative example of both.

Baselines are unusually thorough for this area: direct SFT, STaR rationalization, temperature sweeps, GRPO, NuRL, and GRPO on the 40K DeepScaleR dataset, plus an ablation of the loss components (Table 4) showing the contrastive term outperforms pure distillation-only KL and that the negative-reference-only term degrades performance.

The analysis section is informative: Figure 6's train-vs-test generalization gap nicely supports the shortcut-learning thesis, and the post-hoc deduplication analysis (Appendix A) plus the released IMO proof dataset with documented permission address data hygiene and resource contribution.

The paper is honest about limitations: Appendix material shows mixed results on weaker models (Qwen3-4B, R1-Distill-7B, Figure 16), and the limitations of hyperparameter reuse across models are discussed.
Training efficiency claims are quantified with concrete compute numbers (0.1 vs 277.6 H100-hours/epoch) and the offline/LoRA formulation is a real practical advantage.
weaknesses: Reproducibility is undermined by incompleteness: footnotes 4 and 5 state 'Our extracted training dataset is available at' and 'Our code is available at' with no URL provided, and the appendix does not include seeds or variance estimates; given pass@k curves at n=128, single-seed results without confidence intervals make several claimed gaps (e.g., ~2% pass@128 differences) difficult to assess as significant.

Hyperparameter methodology is weak: τ is selected by qualitative inspection ('select the best performance outside this region') calibrated on training data rather than validation, and γ is tuned on a 100-sample AIME validation set drawn from the same distribution as training — yet a single γ=0.1 is then reused across all settings, including the non-verifiable proof setting where the Appendix admits per-model tuning would likely help. This limits the strength of out-of-domain and cross-model claims.

The mixed policy rollout truncation at 256 tokens for long-CoT reasoning models is under-justified: training on 256-token prefixes of problems requiring thousands of tokens of reasoning is a significant design decision resting only on qualitative judgment, and its interaction with the 2×–4× token-efficiency claims is not analyzed.

The negative reference construction (regex extraction of waypoints) is heuristic and math-specific; the claimed generalization to other domains ('domains where reward signals are sparse or undefined' in the conclusion) is not supported — the only OOD test, GPQA-Diamond, shows pass@1 sometimes below baseline and pass@128 gains of a few points.

Novelty positioning is overclaimed: the statement that this is 'the first demonstration' of improving long-CoT reasoning from expert solutions sits uneasily with the cited concurrent works (BREAD's branched rollouts from expert anchors, Yang et al.'s reference-guided interventions, self-distillation work), and the related-work section does not clearly delineate what is genuinely new beyond combining privileged conditioning with a contrastive negative reference.

Several attributions are speculative rather than demonstrated: e.g., that NuRL underperforms due to 'a learned reliance on hints', or that DAIL's efficiency gains come from 'high information density' in expert traces — no direct evidence (e.g., trace analysis, controlled comparisons) is provided for these causal claims.

Scope is narrow empirically: two 7–8B models on mathematics, with the weaker-model experiments showing mixed/negative results, so the headline claim that DAIL 'enables learning from expert solutions' holds only in a specific capability regime that is characterized post hoc.

strengths: Clear and well-motivated problem framing: learning from expensive expert solutions on problems where RLVR yields zero advantage (including non-verifiable proof problems), a setting of genuine practical importance at the frontier.

The two-component method (privileged-student in-distribution expansion via mixed policy rollouts, plus a contrastive objective against a 'rationalization' negative reference) is coherent, and each component is motivated by a distinct failure mode (didactic vs. rationalization shortcuts).

Comprehensive and well-designed evaluation: baselines span naive imitation (SFT, STaR, temperature sweeps) and RLVR (GRPO, NuRL, GRPO on DeepScaleR), with ablations for the contrastive loss vs. NLL (Table 4), direct sampling vs. mixed policy rollouts (Figure 7), and analysis showing baselines overfit training data while DAIL generalizes (Figure 6).
Release of a new resource (e1-proof: Olympiad proofs authored by an IMO coach, with permission), enabling training and evaluation on non-verifiable proof problems.
Careful treatment of potential data contamination: post-hoc deduplication analysis against IMO-AnswerBench (Figure 14) and proactive SentenceBERT-based deduplication for the proof split.

Honest limitations discussion: the appendix candidly reports that weaker models (Qwen3-4B, R1-Distill-7B) show mixed results and offers plausible explanations, and the contamination analysis is transparent.
Strong efficiency claims backed by analysis: improved performance under reduced token budgets (Figure 4) and a concrete compute comparison (0.1 vs. 277.6 H100-hours per epoch vs. GRPO).
weaknesses: All experiments use 7–8B scale models; it is unclear whether the conclusions (particularly the necessity of in-distribution expansion and the contrastive objective) hold for larger, stronger models, which is the stated target regime ('at the frontier where such a teacher does not exist').

The contrastive objective's negative KL term is theoretically unbounded, and stability is argued only empirically (Appendix B.5); no theoretical or more formal analysis of the objective's behavior is provided.

Several methodological choices are heuristic and math-specific: the negative reference is constructed via regular-expression extraction of waypoints, and τ is calibrated on training-set performance with qualitative filtering; generalization of the negative-reference construction to other domains is not demonstrated.

Ambiguity about truncated rollouts for the reasoning model: Appendix B.2 states long-CoT rollouts are truncated at 256 tokens as a 'qualitatively good stopping point'; it is unclear how such truncated prefixes constitute complete training solutions for Qwen3-8B, and this design choice deserves more justification and analysis.

Hyperparameter concerns: γ = 0.1 was tuned on Qwen2.5 and reused across all models including weaker ones (the authors themselves note this likely hurts the weaker-model results), and validation sets are small (100 samples); sensitivity analysis beyond γ is limited.

Statistical rigor: headline benchmarks are small (60 AIME 2024/2025 problems), and no error bars, confidence intervals, or multiple-seed variance are reported for the fine-tuning results, making 10–25% pass@k gains hard to assess precisely.
Some incompleteness in the manuscript: footnotes 4 and 5 referencing the released dataset and code are empty in this version, which limits reproducibility assessment as submitted.

Minor internal inconsistencies: §3.1 states e1-proof 'consists of 669' problems while Appendix A describes collecting 683 and deduplicating to a 669-problem evaluation set, making the training/evaluation split somewhat confusing.

strengths: Well-motivated and clearly framed problem: RLVR yields zero advantage/gradients on problems the model cannot solve even with high-k sampling, and naive SFT on didactic expert solutions degrades post-trained models. The two-pronged diagnosis (didactic shortcuts in expert solutions; rationalization shortcuts in student-expanded traces) is coherent and well-illustrated (Figure 1).

The method components are sensible and well-motivated: mixed policy rollouts (inspired by speculative decoding / DAgger) to keep traces on-policy while anchoring to expert solutions, and a contrastive KL objective with a cleverly constructed 'negative reference' conditioned on regex-extracted solution waypoints to penalize shortcut-inducing tokens.

Unusually thorough empirical evaluation: comparisons against SFT, STaR rationalization, temperature sweeps, GRPO, NuRL+GRPO, GRPO on DeepScaleR (>40K examples), and distillation from Qwen3-235B; ablations over the contrastive objective vs NLL (Fig. 5, Table 9), direct sampling vs mixed policy rollouts (Fig. 7), gamma and tau calibration, and evaluation across three math benchmarks plus out-of-domain GPQA and non-math tasks (Reasoning Gym, HealthBench, ToolAlpaca).
Honest handling of potential contamination: post-hoc deduplication analysis against IMO-AnswerBench (Fig. 14) showing robustness, and proactive SentenceBERT deduplication for the e1-proof split.

Honest reporting of limitations: DAIL fails on Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct (Table 11) and yields only modest gains on weaker models (Fig. 16), and the appendix candidly discusses an unsuccessful on-policy variant.

Strong efficiency story backed by numbers: offline off-policy training with LoRA costs ~0.1 H100-hours/epoch vs 277.6 for GRPO per epoch, and the method improves reasoning efficiency (2x fewer tokens at matched coverage, Fig. 4).
Reproducibility: prompts, hyperparameters, negative-reference construction details, and released datasets (e1-verifiable, e1-proof) and code.
weaknesses: Methodological novelty is moderate: the ingredients (teacher-conditioned rationalization, speculative-decoding-style interleaved sampling, KL-contrastive objectives) are largely existing techniques recombined for this setting; the negative reference construction via regex waypoint extraction is somewhat ad hoc and may not transfer cleanly to domains without extractable numerical/symbolic waypoints.

The contrastive objective's negative term is theoretically unbounded; stability is argued empirically rather than through analysis, and the comparison to simpler alternatives (e.g., token-weighted NLL that downweights shortcut tokens, or DPO-style preference losses) is missing—only NLL and single-direction KL ablations are provided (Table 9).

No error bars, confidence intervals, or multiple seeds are reported for pass@k results, despite some gaps (e.g., GRPO vs DAIL at small k on IMO-AnswerBench, 6.4 vs 6.8 pass@1) being small relative to plausible sampling variance.

Hyperparameters (gamma on a 100-sample validation set; tau calibrated on training-set performance with qualitative filtering) involve choices that could be slightly overfit, and the tau selection procedure mixes quantitative and qualitative criteria.

The '2x fewer tokens' efficiency claim may be partially confounded: traces are truncated at 256 tokens during generation for reasoning models, which could bias the distilled policy toward shorter reasoning regardless of genuine efficiency gains; no direct analysis disentangles this.

Scale and domain coverage are limited: largest model is 14B, all fine-tuning via LoRA, and the domain is predominantly competition mathematics; the failure on Llama-3.1-8B suggests the approach requires a reasonably competent base model, constraining the claimed generality of 'making expert reasoning learnable.'

Some benchmark-adjacent choices could be scrutinized: e1-verifiable is built from community AoPS solutions (variable quality), and evaluation on AIME 2024/2025 shares format/source style with training data even if problems differ.

strengths: The paper addresses a real and well-motivated problem: RLVR provides no learning signal on problems where the model cannot sample a correct rollout, and naive imitation of expert solutions degrades reasoning. The framing of 'didactic shortcuts' (human omissions) vs. 'rationalization shortcuts' (model hallucinated bridges to known results) is a genuinely useful conceptual contribution.

The evaluation is unusually thorough for this area: temperature-swept baselines (τ ∈ {0.6–1.2}), multiple RLVR baselines including a realistic large-scale DeepScaleR GRPO run, STaR and direct SFT baselines, loss ablations (Table 9), mixed policy vs. direct sampling ablations (Figure 7), a second backbone family (DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Llama-8B, Table 12), non-math domains (Reasoning Gym, HealthBench, ToolAlpaca), and compute accounting (Appendix C.6).

The authors proactively analyze potential data contamination: post-hoc deduplication against IMO-AnswerBench (Appendix A, Figure 14) shows results are robust, and they proactively deduplicate the proof set with SentenceBERT.
Release of the e1-proof dataset of 669 Olympiad problems with expert solutions, with documented permission, is a concrete community resource enabling work on non-verifiable reasoning problems.

The limitations are honestly reported: DAIL fails on Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct (Table 11), gains are modest on smaller models (Figure 16), an on-policy variant converged poorly (C.7), and pass@1 is sometimes slightly worse than the base model. These are not hidden, which is appropriate scientific practice.
weaknesses: The headline gains are concentrated at large k. On AIME 2024/2025, DAIL's pass@1 (8.8) is below the base model (9.8) and roughly at GRPO's level; on IMO-AnswerBench pass@1 drops from 6.8 to 6.4. The paper's value proposition is therefore 'better pass@128 diversity', which is narrower than the abstract's framing suggests, and the mechanism for why a method that slightly hurts pass@1 dramatically improves pass@128 (presumably distributional broadening rather than better reasoning) is not analyzed directly.

Several components are heuristic and under-justified: the negative reference is constructed via regex extraction of 'waypoints' plus an answer-leak prompt; rollout truncation at 256 tokens is justified only qualitatively; τ=0.8 is selected from a training-set sweep excluding the best-performing region based on qualitative judgments. These choices work, but the paper offers little principled understanding of why, and sensitivity analyses are partial.

The contrastive objective (weighted token-level KL to a teacher minus KL to a negative reference) is empirically motivated but theoretically loose; the claim that the negative term remains bounded relies on empirical observation (Appendix C.6/Figure 13) rather than analysis, and the ablation margin over teacher-only KL is modest (46.0 vs 44.0 pass@128).

Differentiation from concurrent self-distillation work (Zhao et al., 2026; Hübötter et al., 2026; Shenfeld et al., 2026; Yang et al., 2024) rests mainly on the problem regime (extremely hard problems, shortcut mitigation), but there is no direct empirical comparison against these closest methods, only against SFT/STaR/RLVR.

The RLVR comparisons are somewhat favorable to the narrative: GRPO is trained on 417 problems deliberately selected to be unsolvable by the base model, a near-degenerate RL setting, while DAIL additionally benefits from concatenated multi-solution AoPS references the baselines never see. The DeepScaleR comparison partially mitigates this but was trained for only one epoch.

Mixed policy rollouts reuse the student's own weights as the 'teacher', so it is unclear how much of the improvement reflects genuine expert knowledge transfer versus generic fine-tuning on self-generated traces anchored to leaked answers; a control fine-tuning on unanchored self-traces of equal length is absent.

strengths: The paper addresses a well-motivated and important problem: RLVR provides no learning signal on problems the model cannot solve, and naive imitation of expert solutions fails because expert traces are didactic and out-of-distribution. The proposed two-part remedy (in-distribution trace generation via mixed policy rollouts + a contrastive objective against an automatically constructed negative reference) is a sensible and clearly articulated solution.

The experimental evaluation is unusually thorough: DAIL is compared against direct SFT, STaR rationalization, GRPO, NuRL+GRPO, GRPO on the 40K DeepScaleR dataset, and distillation from Qwen3-235B-A22B, plus temperature sweeps to rule out inference-parameter artifacts. The baselines cover the most plausible alternative explanations for the gains.

Ablations are substantive rather than cosmetic: contrastive vs. NLL (Figure 5, Table 9), direct sampling vs. mixed policy rollouts split by model type (Figure 7), calibration of the acceptance threshold τ (Figure 11), a γ sweep, and a train-vs-test generalization gap analysis (Figure 6) that directly supports the shortcut-learning hypothesis motivating the method.

The paper demonstrates the method in both verifiable and non-verifiable (Olympiad proof) settings, and contributes two new released datasets (e1-verifiable, e1-proof), with documented permissions. Code and data release supports reproducibility.

Results span multiple axes: pass@k across three math benchmarks, token-budget scaling (Figure 4), model-size scaling, out-of-domain GPQA-Diamond (Table 1), and non-math domains (Reasoning Gym, HealthBench, ToolAlpaca) in the appendix. Deduplication analysis (Figure 14) proactively addresses potential leakage against IMO-AnswerBench.

Limitations are treated honestly and informatively: the Llama-3.1-8B negative result (Table 11), the modest gains on smaller models (Figure 16), and the exploration of an on-policy variant that converged slowly (Appendix C.7) are all disclosed rather than hidden.
weaknesses: No error bars, seeds, or significance testing are reported for any comparison, particularly concerning given that GRPO runs are known to have high variance. Several headline margins (e.g., DAIL vs. GRPO at small k) are small enough that run-to-run variance could matter.

The method induces a pass@1 vs. pass@k tradeoff that is under-discussed: on AIME 2024/2025 pass@1 drops from 9.8 to 8.8 and on IMO-AnswerBench from 6.8 to 6.4. The paper frames pass@k for k≫1 as the practical metric, but the systematic pass@1 regression deserves explicit analysis rather than the general tradeoff citation given.

Main results rely heavily on the Qwen model family; the only non-Qwen result (DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Llama-8B) appears only in the appendix, and the one non-Qwen instruct model tested (Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct) degrades. Generalization of the method across model families is therefore not firmly established.

Several components are heuristic: the negative reference is built from regex-extracted waypoints, and reasoning-model rollouts are truncated at 256 tokens based on qualitative judgment. The ablations mitigate this concern but the sensitivity of results to these choices (other than τ) is not fully characterized.

There is no verification that the expanded traces are mathematically correct; the generation success rate in Figure 11 is measured on training data. The contrastive loss penalizes shortcut tokens but not incorrect derivations that the student may still internalize.

The claim of being the 'first demonstration' of improving long-CoT reasoning from expert solutions is stated cautiously but sits in a crowded space of concurrent self-distillation work (Zhao et al., 2026; Hübotter et al., 2026; Shenfeld et al., 2026); the differentiation is argued but not empirically compared against these concurrent methods.
Training uses LoRA adapters only; it is unclear how the method behaves with full fine-tuning, which is the standard regime for many RLVR comparisons.
